title: MATH2010 Module 02: Vector Equations and the Matrix Equation Ax = b

questions.q: Compute 2(1, 0, -3) - 3(-2, 1, 4). (Vectors are columns written in a row.)
In the linear combination y = c1 v1 + c2 v2 + ... + cp vp, what are the scalars c1, ..., cp called?
questions.explain: The scalars are called the weights. They can be any real numbers, including 0, negatives, and fractions.

questions.q: To decide whether b is a linear combination of v1, v2, v3, which matrix should you row reduce?
choices: The augmented matrix [v1 v2 v3 | b], with v1, v2, v3 as columns and b as the last column
The matrix whose rows are v1, v2, v3, with b added as a fourth row
The augmented matrix [b v1 v2 | v3]
The two-column matrix [v1 + v2 + v3 | b]
questions.explain: The vector equation x1 v1 + x2 v2 + x3 v3 = b has the same solution set as the system with augmented matrix [v1 v2 v3 | b]. The given vectors become the columns. Putting them in as rows is a common mistake.

questions.q: Let v1 = (1, 0, 1), v2 = (-2, 3, -2), v3 = (-6, 7, 5), and b = (11, -5, 9). Is b a linear combination of v1, v2, v3?
choices: Yes. After R3 <- R3 - R1, [v1 v2 v3 | b] is in echelon form and has no row [0 0 0 | nonzero].
No. The echelon form has last row [0 0 11 | -2], and a nonzero right-hand side means the system is inconsistent.
No. The weights come out as fractions, not whole numbers.
You can't tell until the matrix is in reduced echelon form.
questions.explain: R3 <- R3 - R1 gives [[1, -2, -6 | 11], [0, 3, 7 | -5], [0, 0, 11 | -2]]. The last row says 11 x3 = -2, which is fine because its coefficient part is not all zero. Only a row [0 0 0 | nonzero] means inconsistent. Fractional weights are allowed, and ordinary echelon form is enough to decide consistency.

questions.q: Let v1 = (1, 0, 1), v2 = (-2, 3, -2), v3 = (-6, 7, 5), and b = (11, -5, 9). Write b = x1 v1 + x2 v2 + x3 v3. Find x3. (A decimal is fine.)
questions.explain: Row reduce [v1 v2 v3 | b]. R3 <- R3 - R1 gives the row [0 0 11 | -2], so 11 x3 = -2 and x3 = -2/11, about -0.1818. (Back-substituting further gives x2 = -41/33 and x1 = 245/33.)

questions.q: Let a1 = (1, 0, 2), a2 = (2, 1, 3), and b = (4, 1, 7). Which weights satisfy x1 a1 + x2 a2 = b?
choices: No weights work, because b is not a linear combination of a1 and a2
questions.explain: Entry by entry, the equations are x1 + 2x2 = 4, x2 = 1, and 2x1 + 3x2 = 7. So x2 = 1, then x1 = 2, and the third equation checks: 4 + 3 = 7. So b = 2a1 + a2.

questions.q: Let a1 = (1, 0, 2) and a2 = (2, 1, 3). True or false: b = (4, 1, 8) is a linear combination of a1 and a2.
questions.explain: Row reduce [[1, 2 | 4], [0, 1 | 1], [2, 3 | 8]]. R3 <- R3 - 2R1 gives [0, -1 | 0], then R3 <- R3 + R2 gives [0, 0 | 1]. That row says 0 = 1, so the system is inconsistent and b is not a combination of a1 and a2.

questions.q: True or false: if the echelon form of an augmented matrix contains the row [0 0 0 | 0], the system has no solution.
questions.explain: A row [0 0 0 | 0] says 0 = 0, which is always true. It just means a redundant equation or a free variable. Only a row [0 ... 0 | nonzero] makes a system inconsistent.

questions.q: Let u = (1, 2, -1), v = (0, 1, 3), and b = (2, 5, h). For what value of h is b in Span{u, v}?
questions.explain: Row reduce [[1, 0 | 2], [2, 1 | 5], [-1, 3 | h]]. R2 <- R2 - 2R1 gives [0, 1 | 1]. R3 <- R3 + R1 gives [0, 3 | h + 2]. Then R3 <- R3 - 3R2 gives [0, 0 | h - 1]. The system is consistent only when h - 1 = 0, so h = 1. Check: 2u + v = (2, 5, 1).

questions.q: Let u = (-1, 1, 4), v = (2, -1, -2), and b = (1, 2, h). For what value of h is b in the plane spanned by u and v?
questions.explain: Row reduce [u v | b]. R2 <- R2 + R1 and R3 <- R3 + 4R1 give rows [0, 1 | 3] and [0, 6 | h + 4]. Then R3 <- R3 - 6R2 gives [0, 0 | h - 14]. The system is consistent only when h = 14. Check: 5u + 3v = (1, 2, 14).

questions.q: For what value of k is (-2, k) in Span{(4, -6)}?
questions.explain: We need (-2, k) = c(4, -6). The first entry forces c = -1/2, and then k = (-1/2)(-6) = 3.

questions.q: Let u and v be nonzero vectors in R^3 that are not multiples of each other. What is Span{u, v}?
choices: A plane through the origin
A line through the origin
All of R^3
A plane that does not have to pass through the origin
questions.explain: Two vectors in R^3 that are not multiples of each other span a plane through the origin. A span always contains 0 (take all weights 0), so it always passes through the origin. Two vectors can never span all of R^3.

questions.q: Let u be a nonzero vector in R^3 and let v = -3u. True or false: Span{u, v} is a plane.
questions.explain: Because v is a multiple of u, it adds no new direction. Every combination c1 u + c2 v = (c1 - 3c2)u is a multiple of u, so Span{u, v} is the line through the origin in the direction of u.

questions.q: True or false: the zero vector is in Span{v1, ..., vp} for any vectors v1, ..., vp.
questions.explain: Take every weight equal to 0: 0 v1 + ... + 0 vp = 0.

questions.q: Let u and v be vectors in R^3, and let b contain an unknown h. Why must at least one value of h make b fail to be in Span{u, v}?
choices: [u v] has only 2 columns, so it has at most 2 pivots and can't have a pivot in all 3 rows. A plane (or line) can't contain every vector of R^3.
A vector that contains a parameter can never be in a span.
u and v must be multiples of each other.
Row reduction always produces the row [0 0 | 1] when there is a parameter.
questions.explain: Two vectors in R^3 give a 3 x 2 coefficient matrix, which has at most 2 pivots. Without a pivot in every row, some right-hand sides make the system inconsistent. Geometrically, Span{u, v} is at most a plane, so it can't contain all of R^3.

questions.q: Let A = [a1 a2 a3] be a 3 x 3 matrix and let b be a vector in R^3. Which statements mean exactly the same thing as "b is in Span{a1, a2, a3}"?
choices: b is a linear combination of a1, a2, a3
The equation Ax = b has a solution
The system with augmented matrix [a1 a2 a3 | b] is consistent
A has a pivot position in every row
The echelon form of [a1 a2 a3 | b] has a pivot in its last column
questions.explain: For a single b, being in the span, being a linear combination of the columns, Ax = b having a solution, and [A | b] being consistent all say the same thing. A pivot in every row of A is a stronger condition: it means every b works, not just this one. A pivot in the last column of [A | b] means the system is inconsistent.

questions.q: Let A have rows (1, 0, 2), (2, 3, -1), (-1, 7, 0), and let x = (2, 3, -5). Find Ax.
questions.explain: Row-vector rule. Row 1: 2 + 0 - 10 = -8. Row 2: 4 + 9 + 5 = 18 (note (-1)(-5) = +5). Row 3: -2 + 21 + 0 = 19. Column check: 2(1, 2, -1) + 3(0, 3, 7) - 5(2, -1, 0) = (-8, 18, 19). The answer (13, -26, 1) comes from combining the rows instead of the columns.

questions.q: Let A be the 2 x 3 matrix with rows (3, -1, 0) and (1, 2, -4), and let x = (2, -1, 1). Find Ax.
choices: Undefined, because A has 2 rows but x has 3 entries
questions.explain: Ax is defined because A has 3 columns and x has 3 entries. The result is in R^2. Row 1: 6 + 1 + 0 = 7. Row 2: 2 - 2 - 4 = -4. So Ax = (7, -4).

questions.q: A is a 3 x 5 matrix and the product Ax is defined. Which space is x in, and which space is Ax in?
choices: x is in R^5 and Ax is in R^3
x is in R^3 and Ax is in R^5
x is in R^5 and Ax is in R^5
x is in R^3 and Ax is in R^3
questions.explain: Ax needs x to have one entry for each column of A, so x is in R^5. The result has one entry for each row of A, so Ax is in R^3. In general, an m x n matrix times a vector in R^n gives a vector in R^m.

questions.q: Let A have rows (4, -2, 1), (-3, 0, 5), (1, 6, -2), and let x = (2, -1, -3). What is the second entry of Ax?
questions.explain: Use row 2 of A with the entries of x: (-3)(2) + (0)(-1) + (5)(-3) = -6 + 0 - 15 = -21.

questions.q: Let A be the 3 x 2 matrix with rows (2, -1), (0, 3), (1, 1). Which vector equation is equivalent to Ax = b?
questions.explain: Ax = x1 a1 + x2 a2, where a1 and a2 are the columns of A. The columns are (2, 0, 1) and (-1, 3, 1). The second choice wrongly uses the rows as vectors.

questions.q: A is a matrix with Au = (1, 2) and Av = (3, -1). What is A(2u - v)?
choices: It can't be determined without knowing A
questions.explain: Use A(u + v) = Au + Av and A(cu) = c(Au): A(2u - v) = 2Au - Av = (2, 4) - (3, -1) = (-1, 5).

questions.q: True or false: Ax is the linear combination of the columns of A that uses the entries of x as the weights.
questions.explain: This is the definition: if A = [a1 ... an], then Ax = x1 a1 + x2 a2 + ... + xn an.

questions.q: Let I be the 3 x 3 identity matrix (1s on the diagonal, 0s elsewhere). True or false: Ix = x for every x in R^3.

Let A have rows (1, 2, 3), (-1, 5, -4), (-1, 19, -6). Row reducing [A | b] with b = (b1, b2, b3) gives [[1, 2, 3 | b1], [0, 7, -1 | b1 + b2], [0, 0, 0 | -2b1 - 3b2 + b3]]. Why does Ax = b not have a solution for every b?
choices: A has no pivot in row 3, so some b (for example b = (0, 0, 1)) make the last row read 0 = nonzero.
A has more columns than rows.
The last row is [0 0 0 | 0] for every b.
Ax = b has no solution for any b.
questions.explain: The coefficient matrix has only two pivots and none in row 3. Whenever -2b1 - 3b2 + b3 is not 0, the last row is a contradiction. With b = (0, 0, 1) it reads 0 = 1. A is square (3 x 3), and some b do work (b = 0, for example).

questions.q: Let A have rows (1, 2, 3), (-1, 5, -4), (-1, 19, -6). Which description gives exactly the set of b = (b1, b2, b3) for which Ax = b has a solution?
choices: All b with 2b1 + 3b2 - b3 = 0, a plane through the origin
All of R^3
All b with -2b1 - 3b2 + b3 not equal to 0
questions.explain: Row reduction (R2 <- R2 + R1, R3 <- R3 + R1, then R3 <- R3 - 3R2) leaves the last row [0 0 0 | -2b1 - 3b2 + b3]. The system is consistent exactly when that entry is 0, which means b3 = 2b1 + 3b2. This is a plane through the origin, and it equals the span of the columns of A.

questions.q: Let A have rows (1, 2, 3), (-1, 5, -4), (-1, 19, -6). For what value of k does Ax = b have a solution when b = (1, -1, k)?
questions.explain: Ax = b is solvable exactly when b3 = 2b1 + 3b2. Here that gives k = 2(1) + 3(-1) = -1.

questions.q: Let A have rows (1, 2, 3), (-1, 5, -4), (-1, 19, -6). For which of these vectors b does Ax = b have a solution?
questions.explain: The condition is b3 = 2b1 + 3b2. (1, 0, 2): 2 = 2, yes. (1, 1, 4): 5 is not 4, no. (0, 0, 1): 0 is not 1, no. (2, -1, 1): 4 - 3 = 1, yes. (3, -4, -6): 6 - 12 = -6, yes. This last one is the third column of A, so it has to work.

questions.q: Let A be the 2 x 2 matrix with rows (1, 2) and (3, 6). For which b = (b1, b2) does Ax = b have a solution?
choices: Exactly those with b2 = 3b1
Exactly those with b1 = 3b2
Exactly those with b2 = 2b1
Every b in R^2, because A is square
questions.explain: Row reduce [[1, 2 | b1], [3, 6 | b2]]. R2 <- R2 - 3R1 gives [0, 0 | b2 - 3b1]. The system is consistent exactly when b2 - 3b1 = 0. A square matrix does not automatically have a pivot in every row.

questions.q: Let A be the 3 x 2 matrix with rows (1, 0), (0, 1), (2, -1). For what value of k does Ax = b have a solution when b = (3, 1, k)?
questions.explain: Row reduce [A | b]. R3 <- R3 - 2R1 + R2 turns the last row into [0, 0 | b3 - 2b1 + b2]. So the condition is b3 = 2b1 - b2, which gives k = 2(3) - 1 = 5. Check: x = (3, 1) gives Ax = (3, 1, 6 - 1) = (3, 1, 5).

questions.q: True or false: if the echelon form of [A | b] has a pivot in its last (augmented) column, then Ax = b has no solution.
questions.explain: A pivot in the augmented column means a row [0 ... 0 | nonzero], which says 0 = nonzero. That is why the test for "solvable for every b" looks for a pivot in every row of A, not of [A | b].

questions.q: Let A have rows (2, 2, 4), (-1, 3, -2), (-4, -4, 5). Do the columns of A span R^3, and does Ax = b have a solution for every b in R^3?
choices: Yes to both. R2 <- R2 + (1/2)R1 and R3 <- R3 + 2R1 give an echelon form with pivots 2, 4, 13, one in every row.
No to both. The echelon form of A has a row of zeros.
The columns span R^3, but Ax = b still fails for some b.
You can't tell without a specific b.
questions.explain: Row reducing A gives rows (2, 2, 4), (0, 4, 0), (0, 0, 13). A has a pivot in every row, so by the existence theorem its columns span R^3 and Ax = b is consistent for every b. The two questions always have the same answer, and you only need to reduce A.

questions.q: Let u = (-1, 0, 2), v = (-1, 5, 0), w = (2, -1, 7), and b = (c, d, h). Row reducing [u v w | b] gives [[-1, -1, 2 | c], [0, 5, -1 | d], [0, 0, 53 | 10c + 2d + 5h]]. What does this show?
choices: b is in Span{u, v, w} for every c, d, h, because the coefficient part has a pivot in every row, so no row [0 0 0 | nonzero] can appear
b is in Span{u, v, w} only when 10c + 2d + 5h = 0
b is in Span{u, v, w} only when c = d = h = 0
Nothing can be concluded until c, d, h are given numbers
questions.explain: The last row has coefficient part (0, 0, 53), not all zeros, so it just determines x3 = (10c + 2d + 5h)/53. With pivots -1, 5, 53 in every row, the system is consistent for every c, d, h, so Span{u, v, w} = R^3. Setting the right-hand side to 0 would only be needed if the coefficient part of that row were all zeros.

questions.q: True or false: the vectors (1, 1, 0), (0, 1, 1), (1, 0, 1) span R^3.
questions.explain: Put them in as columns: rows (1, 0, 1), (1, 1, 0), (0, 1, 1). R2 <- R2 - R1 gives (0, 1, -1). Then R3 <- R3 - R2 gives (0, 0, 2). There is a pivot in every row, so the columns span R^3.

choices: No. The matrix with these columns reduces to an echelon form with a zero row, so there is no pivot in row 3.
Yes. Three vectors in R^3 always span R^3.
Yes. None of the vectors is a multiple of another.
No. A vector with a negative entry can't be part of a spanning set.
questions.explain: The matrix has rows (1, 2, 0), (-1, 1, 3), (2, 1, -3). R2 <- R2 + R1 gives (0, 3, 3). R3 <- R3 - 2R1 gives (0, -3, -3). Then R3 <- R3 + R2 gives (0, 0, 0). There is no pivot in row 3, so they don't span R^3. In fact the third vector equals the second minus twice the first, so the span is only a plane. None of the vectors being a multiple of another is not enough.

questions.q: True or false: any three vectors in R^3 span R^3.
questions.explain: Counterexample: the columns of the matrix with rows (1, 2, 3), (-1, 5, -4), (-1, 19, -6). That matrix has only 2 pivots, and its columns span only the plane 2b1 + 3b2 - b3 = 0. You always have to check for a pivot in every row.

questions.q: True or false: if the three columns of a 4 x 3 matrix are chosen well, they can span R^4.
questions.explain: A 4 x 3 matrix has at most 3 pivots (at most one per column), so it can't have a pivot in all 4 rows. When a matrix has more rows than columns, its columns can never span R^m.

questions.q: Do four vectors in R^3 span R^3?
choices: It depends. They span R^3 exactly when the 3 x 4 matrix with these vectors as columns has a pivot in every row.
Always, because there are more vectors than entries.
Never, because the matrix with these vectors as columns is not square.
questions.explain: The existence theorem applies to any m x n matrix: the columns span R^m exactly when there is a pivot in every row. A 3 x 4 matrix may or may not have 3 pivots. For example, four multiples of the same vector span only a line.

questions.q: A is an m x n matrix. Which conditions guarantee that the columns of A span R^m?
choices: A has a pivot position in every row
Ax = b has a solution for every b in R^m
Every b in R^m is a linear combination of the columns of A
Ax = 0 has a solution
A has more columns than rows
[A | b] has a pivot in every row for some particular b
questions.explain: By the existence theorem, the first three statements are equivalent to the columns spanning R^m. Ax = 0 always has the solution x = 0, so it guarantees nothing. Having more columns than rows does not ensure a pivot in every row. A pivot in every row of [A | b] can include a pivot in the last column, which means that system is inconsistent.

questions.q: True or false: to show that u, v, w span R^3, it is enough to row reduce the coefficient matrix [u v w], with no right-hand side, and find a pivot in every row.
questions.explain: The pivot positions depend only on the coefficient columns. A pivot in every row of [u v w] means no contradiction row can appear for any right-hand side b, so every b in R^3 is in Span{u, v, w}.
